analysis.one_liner: Shifts $60 billion from defense and nuclear weapons spending to schools, children's health coverage, job training, and clean energy.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote in the House; it sat in six committees after referral until the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have cut $47 billion from the Department of Defense and $13 billion from Department of Energy nuclear security programs for fiscal year 2008. It would have redirected that money to school repair and construction, children's health coverage through the State Children's Health Insurance Program, job training for unemployed and dislocated workers, energy efficiency and renewable energy programs, humanitarian and development aid, homeland security improvements, veterans health care, and deficit reduction.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the bill would have funded school modernization in districts with crumbling buildings, expanded children's health coverage through SCHIP, added job training for dislocated workers, increased federal investment in energy efficiency and renewables, and added $3 billion for veterans' health care.

how_it_helps.text: Provides $10 billion to modernize public school facilities, responding to GAO estimates that one-third of the nation's public schools serving 14 million children need extensive repair or replacement [S3].
Provides $9 billion to state child health plans under SCHIP, aimed at the more than 9 million children the bill's findings say lack health insurance for an entire year [S3].
Provides $5 billion for employment and training of adult and dislocated workers, apportioned by the Department of Labor on a per capita job loss basis [S3].
Provides $10 billion for energy efficiency, conservation, and sustainable and renewable energy programs [S3].
Provides $3 billion for veterans' health care and $5 billion for deficit reduction, in addition to school, health, and training funding [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Defense contractors and the Department of Energy's nuclear weapons programs would have absorbed the $60 billion in cuts, which the bill drew from weapons programs its findings called obsolete, including Cold War-era weapons systems, space weapons development, and nuclear arsenal maintenance.
analysis.who_pays_short: Defense contractors and nuclear weapons programs

drawbacks.text: Cutting $47 billion from the Department of Defense in a single year, during the Iraq and Afghanistan wars, could have affected military readiness, weapons procurement, and defense-dependent communities and jobs [S3].

The bill mandates fixed dollar reallocations across six jurisdictions at once, leaving funding levels to be set by secretaries rather than tested through the normal appropriations process, which would have made the transfers hard to adjust to changing conditions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefits were large and broadly shared: school repairs, children's coverage, job training, and clean energy investment reaching millions of people. The main cost fell on defense and nuclear weapons spending, which the bill's own findings characterized as exceeding that of 192 other countries combined and including weapons with no current adversary [S3]. An honest objection is the speed and rigidity of the cut and the disruption it would have caused to defense programs and jobs, particularly while two wars were underway. The bill offered no phase-in period beyond a 90-day effective date [S3].

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to six committees on the day it was introduced; subcommittees took no action, and the bill died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009 without ever reaching the floor.

narrative.text: Representative Lynn Woolsey introduced the bill on March 26, 2007, with 22 original cosponsors [S3].
The bill was referred to six House committees at once: Armed Services, Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, Homeland Security, Foreign Affairs, and Veterans' Affairs [S1].

Between March and July 2007 it was referred to five subcommittees, including subcommittees handling health, energy, veterans' economic opportunity, and education; no committee ever reported the bill [S5].
The bill accumulated 44 cosponsors, all Democrats, and received no vote in either chamber before the Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Defense programs and their contractors kept the full fiscal year 2008 funding the bill would have cut, and no committee had to weigh the reallocation. Children lacking insurance, schools needing repairs, and dislocated workers saw none of the proposed funding.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Defense programs kept their funding untouched

for.name: Rep. Lynn Woolsey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and framed it as a transfer from what she called wasteful defense spending to schools, children's health, and job training [S3].

for.name: 45 of 233 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and cosponsored the bill, all 45 of them Democrats [S4].

against.name: House Armed Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and never reported it out; no markup or vote appears in the action history [S5].

against.name: Five other House committees of referral
against.role: Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, Homeland Security, Foreign Affairs, Veterans' Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by sequential referral and never acted on it beyond routing pieces of it to subcommittees [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All 45 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican supported the bill; the record shows no floor vote at which positions could have split further [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have cut $47 billion from Department of Defense fiscal 2008 appropriations, much of which flows to weapons procurement and contractors. Its findings targeted spending on Cold War-era weapons systems and space weapons development [S3].

industries.industry: Nuclear weapons complex and DOE national security contractors
industries.note: The bill would have cut $13 billion from Department of Energy national security programs, which maintain the nuclear arsenal, redirecting the money to domestic priorities [S3].

industries.industry: Renewable energy and energy efficiency firms
industries.note: The bill would have directed $10 billion to the Energy Secretary for efficiency, conservation, and renewable energy investment, expanding demand for these industries [S3].
The bill would have provided $10 billion for school modernization under the Elementary and Secondary Education Act, funding repairs and replacement of facilities [S3].
